project.name: How to Train Your AI
project.description: A Java Swing group course project (CMSC 170): a Who-Wants-to-Be-a-Millionaire-style AI-themed quiz game, currently in early Week 1 of a 5-week build.

nodes.name: Question Bank
nodes.summary: Legacy comma-delimited draft question bank (769 rows) with per-member AI-themed multiple-choice questions tagged by Bloom's Taxonomy level (Knowledge/Understanding/Application/Analysis/Evaluation/Synthesis); superseded by the pipe-delimited MCQ/*.csv format decided in CONTEXT.md, with content still to be ported rather than discarded.

nodes.name: TurnResult.java
nodes.summary: Immutable data object describing the outcome of one submitted answer -- correctness, tokens awarded, running total, capability-unlock status/name, and whether the session ended -- consumed by the GUI to render feedback after each turn.

nodes.name: TurnResult
nodes.summary: Immutable value object holding the result of one turn: correctness, tokens awarded this turn and running total, capability-unlock flag/name, and game-over flag, exposed via simple getters with no logic of its own.

nodes.name: Choice.java
nodes.summary: Represents one answer option for a Question, preserving the original CSV letter (a-d) as a stable identifier independent of the order choices are shuffled for display.

nodes.name: Choice
nodes.summary: Immutable pairing of a stable choiceId letter and its display text, used so shuffled on-screen ordering never breaks correctness checks against the original CSV letter.

nodes.name: Question.java
nodes.summary: Represents one multiple-choice question loaded from an MCQ data source, holding its module, Bloom level, text, explanation, shuffled choices, and the correct choice id, with an isCorrect() helper to check submitted answers.

nodes.name: Question
nodes.summary: Immutable question record with id, module, Bloom level, text, explanation, choice list, and correct-choice id; isCorrect(choiceId) checks an answer against the original pre-shuffle letter.

tour.title: Project Source of Truth
tour.description: CONTEXT.md is the project's actual source of truth, not the generic VS Code README you'll find elsewhere in the repo. It captures the game proposal, the assignment requirements it must satisfy, the team's execution plan, and — critically — the locked decision on the CSV data format used for questions. Start here to understand what this project is (an AI-themed, Who-Wants-to-Be-a-Millionaire-style quiz game) before looking at any code.

tour.title: Team Execution Plan
tour.description: Building on Step 1, this document explains HOW the team is building the project: four defined roles, a pre-coding agreement to lock the CSV question format before anyone writes loading code, shared-class scaffolding built first so members can work in parallel, and a week-by-week schedule with integration gates. This explains why you'll see interfaces and placeholder classes throughout the codebase instead of finished logic — the project is in Week 1 of 5, and this plan is the reason the scaffolding looks the way it does.

tour.title: Application Entry Point
tour.description: Main.java is where the program starts. It bootstraps the Swing GUI and wires up navigation between screens using a CardPanel-based router, importing all five GUI panels (CardPanel, MainMenuPanel, PlayPanel, SettingsPanel, TutorialPanel) directly. As the plan from Step 2 promised, this is shared scaffolding: it exists so every team member has a working app shell to build their piece into.
tour.languageLesson: Java Swing applications conventionally start from a main() method that constructs the top-level JFrame and adds child components before calling setVisible(true) — everything downstream is reachable from this one bootstrap point.

tour.title: The Screen Router
tour.description: CardPanel wraps Swing's CardLayout to let the app register named screens and switch which one is visible without destroying and recreating components. Main.java (Step 3) hands every panel to this router, and each panel later calls back into it to navigate elsewhere — for example, MainMenuPanel's Play button will tell CardPanel to show the play screen. This indirection is what lets four different screens be developed independently without needing to know about each other directly.
tour.languageLesson: CardLayout is a Swing layout manager that stacks components like a deck of cards, showing only one at a time by string key — a lightweight alternative to a full navigation framework, well suited to a small multi-screen desktop app.

tour.title: The Four Screens
tour.description: These four panels are the screens registered with CardPanel from Step 4. MainMenuPanel is the most built-out, with working Play/Settings/Tutorial/Exit buttons, while PlayPanel, SettingsPanel, and TutorialPanel are currently placeholders — just a title and a back button. This is deliberate Week 1 scaffolding: the navigation skeleton exists end-to-end so that whoever implements the actual quiz gameplay, settings, or tutorial content later only has to fill in one panel's body, not rebuild the app's screen-switching logic.

tour.title: Question and Choice Data Model
tour.description: Stepping away from the GUI, Question and Choice are the immutable data classes that represent quiz content. A Question carries an id, module, Bloom's-taxonomy difficulty level, text, explanation, and a list of shuffled Choices plus the id of the correct one, exposing an isCorrect() check. Choice keeps a stable original-letter choiceId separate from its display text specifically so that shuffling the on-screen order never breaks the answer key — a small but important design decision for a game where choice order should be randomized per session.
tour.languageLesson: Both classes are immutable value objects (fields set once via constructor, no setters) — a common Java pattern for data that's shared across threads or passed freely between GUI and engine code without risk of accidental mutation.

tour.title: The Question Source Contract
tour.description: QuestionSource is an interface with a single method, buildSession(), which is contracted to return exactly 15 Questions (Step 6) in ascending Bloom-level order with their choices already shuffled. No implementation exists yet — this interface is a seam the rest of the system can be built against before the real question-loading logic (reading from the CSV/JSON data you'll see next) is written. It's the same pre-coding-agreement approach described in Step 2's plan: agree on the shape first, implement in parallel second.
tour.languageLesson: Programming to an interface lets teammates write code against QuestionSource's contract immediately, then swap in a real CSV- or JSON-backed implementation later without changing any calling code — a classic dependency-inversion pattern.

tour.title: Game Engine Session Contracts
tour.description: GameEngine is the interface the GUI will eventually call to run a quiz session: startSession, currentQuestion, submitAnswer, and endSession. It depends on three supporting value types — Protocol (a placeholder enum for STANDARD vs. HIGH_RISK session modes), TurnResult (the immutable outcome of one turn: correctness, tokens awarded, capability unlocks, game-over flag), and SessionResult (an empty placeholder reserved for Week 4's finished-session summary). Together with QuestionSource from Step 7, this is the full 'seam' the GUI panels from Step 5 will eventually be wired against once the real engine logic is implemented.
tour.languageLesson: Java enums like Protocol are more than named constants — they can carry fields and methods, making them a good fit for modeling a small closed set of session modes that may later need associated behavior.

tour.title: The Current Question Bank Data
tour.description: week01.json is the actual data QuestionSource (Step 7) and Question (Step 6) will eventually be built to load — the 'Introduction to Artificial Intelligence' module's question bank in the current, agreed-upon format. This is the concrete payload behind the abstract interfaces you just saw: once someone implements QuestionSource, this file (and others like it per week) is what buildSession() will read from disk.

tour.title: The Superseded Legacy Format
tour.description: This CSV file is the team's original, comma-delimited draft question bank — documented in both CONTEXT.md and the execution plan from Steps 1-2 as the format that was superseded by the pipe-delimited MCQ/*.csv (and now JSON, as seen in Step 9) format. It's kept in the repo as a record of the format-lock decision: comparing this legacy draft to week01.json shows concretely why the team paused to agree on a data format before writing any loading code, avoiding rework once multiple people started producing question content in parallel.
tour.languageLesson: CSV format choices matter early: a comma delimiter breaks on any answer text that itself contains a comma, which is likely why the team's locked format switched to a pipe delimiter — a small decision with outsized downstream effects on parser robustness.
